problem: LLM planners such as SayCan and Code-as-Policies reason only over text, with no visual grounding. They hand low-level execution to skill models (RT-1/RT-2) that generalize poorly to new objects and robot morphologies. Prior affordance, contact-point and grasp-preference predictors are task- or object-specific and hard to combine for multi-object, multi-stage household tasks.
motivation: MLLMs such as GPT-4V understand scenes and object properties well, while classical robot stacks are good at precise trajectory planning and execution. Code can act as a symbolic, robot-agnostic bridge between the two. Existing MLLM pretraining focuses on vision-language alignment and does not cover physical preferences (grasp direction, articulation constraints) or the multi-source reasoning needed to write robot code.
key_idea: Train a BLIP-2-style vision-language model (EVA-CLIP ViT-G + Q-Former + LLaMA-13B) to generate tree-of-thought robot code. The code decomposes an instruction into object-centric units, and each unit calls perception, affordance, articulation, grasp-preference and motion-planning APIs. Training uses GPT-4-synthesized code and an iterative self-updating SFT loop driven by execution search.
insight: The gains over GPT-4V on manipulation come mainly from better physical grounding (grasp preference, articulation direction) rather than better task decomposition. The failure analysis (Fig. errorbar) shows both RoboCodeX and GPT-4V decompose long-horizon tasks correctly; most errors come from suboptimal grasp-pose selection and the trajectory-planning failures that follow from it. RoboCodeX reduces exactly these errors. Ablations, reported only as figures, show three things: using predicted preferences to pick among AnyGrasp's top-10 candidates clearly beats taking the highest-scoring grasp; the multi-scale vision adapter helps but matters less; and mixing general VQA data into SFT is essential, since without it the model overfits and stops following instructions.
method: Multi-view 3D perception: three RGB-D views (left/right/top) are fused into a TSDF. GLIP 2D detections are matched across views using depth geometry and lifted to 3D boxes, object point clouds and an occupancy map.

Tree-of-thought code generation: the MLLM takes three RGB views plus the instruction and outputs object-centric units, each with a sub-task description L_i and a manipulation preference pf_i (preferred position, approach direction, plane normal), written as Python code with comment annotations over ROS/MoveIt APIs.

Per-unit expansion via API tools: (i) part-level affordance segmentation (e.g., a handle); (ii) AnyGrasp top-10 grasp proposals, from which the preference picks one (alternative: 'central_lift' top-down grasp); (iii) physical properties from GAMMA (PointNet++ articulation segmentation and joint-axis regression, fine-tuned on multi-view point clouds) plus Open3D plane normals; (iv) trajectory planning with MoveIt/OMPL and zeroth-order sampling scored by S_control under occupancy-map collision constraints, executed as end-effector waypoints by an operational-space controller.

Pretraining data: procedurally populated HM3D scenes with objects from Google Scanned, YCB, OmniObject3D and AKB-48. GPT-4 writes free-form tasks and code from text scene descriptions; 10 code samples are drawn per task, rated by GPT-3.5 and syntax-filtered. This is mixed with ShareGPT4V, SViT and LLaVA-Instruct-150K.

Iterative self-updating SFT: task types come from RT-1 and LIBERO, combined with diverse objects. GPT-4 writes code from human examples. When code executes but fails, an exhaustive search runs over grasp method, contact position, gripper direction and trajectory mode; the best option becomes the label, with a GPT-4V-written rationale as chain-of-thought. Codes that still score zero are hand-fixed and added to the example pool. ShareGPT4V SFT data is mixed in.

Vision adapter: the ViT layers are split into 4 stages and the CLS token of each stage is taken. These tokens pass through a channel-wise attention MLP (Linear→SiLU→Linear→LayerNorm) and are concatenated with the Q-Former visual tokens, which compress vision to leave room for long API-doc prompts.

setting.backbone: RoboCodeX-13B: EVA-CLIP ViT-G/14 (frozen) + Q-Former + LLaMA-13B, BLIP-2 architecture, with Q-Former/LLM fine-tuned. Paired with GLIP-L, AnyGrasp and GAMMA as tool modules.
setting.training_data: Pretraining: GPT-4-generated multimodal robot-code dataset on procedurally populated HM3D scenes (objects from Google Scanned, YCB, OmniObject3D, AKB-48), plus ShareGPT4V, SViT and LLaVA-Instruct-150K. SFT: RT-1/LIBERO-style tasks with GPT-4 code refined by execution search, GPT-4V CoT annotations and human fixes, plus the ShareGPT4V SFT subset. Dataset scale not reported. No navigation-specific training.
setting.observation: Manipulation: 3 RGB-D views (left, right, top). Navigation: egocentric RGB-D within the L3MVN framework.
setting.action_space: Manipulation: generated Python code calling ROS/MoveIt APIs, producing 6-DoF end-effector waypoint trajectories plus gripper open/close. Navigation: frontier selection (which frontier to explore) inside L3MVN.
setting.simulator: Gazebo + ROS/MoveIt (manipulation); Habitat with HM3D and HSSD scenes (ObjectNav)
setting.privileged: None stated. Relies on external perception modules (GLIP, AnyGrasp, GAMMA) and hand-designed APIs rather than GT info.

numbers_note: The ObjectNav split and episode counts are not stated. 'val' is assumed because the HM3D baseline numbers (L3MVN 35.2/16.5, Pixel-Nav 37.9/20.5, ESC 39.2/22.3) match those reported in ESC on the HM3D ObjectNav val set. Pick-and-place per-category results, all ablations (preference, vision adapter, G-VQA data) and the failure-mode analysis appear only in figures, with no numbers in the text. Real-world Franka/UR5 results are qualitative (figures only).
results: On the custom Gazebo manipulation suite (50 trials per task), RoboCodeX beats GPT-4V+GLIP on every task: pick & place 0.80 vs 0.63 (the '17%' headline), drawers 0.84 vs 0.68, doors 0.74 vs 0.52, put-in-drawer 0.68 vs 0.55, multi-stage 0.64 vs 0.50. As the frontier selector inside L3MVN, it reaches ObjectNav SR/SPL of 40.0/24.2 on HM3D, narrowly beating ESC (GPT-3.5) at 39.2/22.3 and Pixel-Nav (GPT-4) at 37.9/20.5. On HSSD it reaches 40.3/22.0 vs L3MVN's 38.4/19.4. It keeps general VQA ability: LLaVA-Bench 71.5 vs LLaVA-1.5-13B's 70.7, though MM-Vet is lower at 31.0 vs 35.4.
limitations: Navigation is a thin add-on: RoboCodeX only replaces the LLM frontier selector in L3MVN, and the paper gives no details on prompts, split, episode count or how candidate frontiers are shown to the model. Gains over ESC are small (+0.8 SR on HM3D).

Heavy reliance on hand-engineered modules and APIs (GLIP, AnyGrasp, GAMMA, Open3D planes, MoveIt/OMPL) and on open-loop generated code. The benchmark is a custom Gazebo suite with 50 trials per task and no standard manipulation benchmark.
Real-world cross-robot results (Franka, UR5) and all ablations are shown only qualitatively or in figures without numbers. Training data scale is not reported.
